title: N-Queens
description:
# N-Queens

The **n-queens** puzzle asks you to place `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard so that no two queens attack each other.

Given an integer `n`, return all distinct solutions to the n-queens puzzle. You may return the list of solutions in any order.

Each solution is an `n`-row board. In every row string, `'Q'` represents a queen and `'.'` represents an empty square. A valid board must contain exactly one queen in each row, and no two queens may share a column, a main diagonal, or an anti-diagonal.

A queen attacks along its row, column, and both diagonal directions. No two queens may share a row, column, or diagonal.

## Example 1:

**Input:** n = 4
**Output:** [[".Q..","...Q","Q...","..Q."],["..Q.","Q...","...Q",".Q.."]]
**Explanation:** There are exactly two distinct valid placements for 4 queens.

## Example 2:

**Input:** n = 1
**Output:** [["Q"]]

## Constraints:

* `1 <= n <= 9`

solutions.name: Backtracking with Sets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Place queens one row at a time. Keep three sets for occupied columns, main diagonals `row - col`, and anti-diagonals `row + col`. A candidate square is legal only when none of those three sets already contains its attack line.

## Key Insight

Because we decide exactly one queen per row, row conflicts are impossible by construction. The whole safety check reduces to columns and the two diagonal families.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n!), because each row can use only one remaining column and invalid branches are pruned early
- Space Complexity: O(n) excluding the returned boards

solutions.name: Backtracking with Boolean Arrays
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use boolean arrays instead of hash sets. `columns[col]` marks occupied columns, `mainDiagonals[row - col + n - 1]` marks one diagonal family, and `antiDiagonals[row + col]` marks the other.

## Key Insight

The same attack lines can be encoded as direct array indexes. This keeps the search logic identical to the set version while removing hashing overhead and making diagonal ranges explicit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n!)
- Space Complexity: O(n) excluding the returned boards

solutions.name: Bitmask Backtracking
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent occupied columns and diagonals as bit masks. For each row, compute all available columns with one mask expression, then repeatedly take the least significant available bit and recurse.

## Key Insight

A board with `n <= 9` fits comfortably in integer masks. Shifting the diagonal masks when moving to the next row carries each attack line into the columns it threatens next.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n!)
- Space Complexity: O(n) recursion depth and board storage, excluding returned boards

solutions.name: Permutation Enumeration with Diagonal Filter
solutions.description:
## Approach

Generate permutations of the column order in ascending-column recursion. In one permutation, row `r` places its queen at `columns[r]`, so row and column conflicts are already impossible. After a full permutation is built, reject it if two rows share a diagonal; otherwise build the board.

## Key Insight

N-Queens can be separated into two constraints. A permutation solves the row-and-column part first, then a diagonal filter handles the remaining attack rules. This is slower than pruning diagonals during search but useful as a teaching baseline.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n! * n), because every permutation may need an O(n) diagonal check
- Space Complexity: O(n) excluding returned boards

tests.description: n = 4 is the canonical case with exactly two valid board arrangements.
n = 1 has the single trivial queen placement.
n = 5 verifies the non-trivial ten-solution case and deeper search output.
